children: By Max Colchester
LONDON-Nearly three decades after Princess Diana's death, her legacy is once again shaking the foundations of the House of Windsor.

A memoir published this week by her younger brother, Charles Spencer, has reopened old wounds and forced the royal family into a damage-limitation exercise, after he alleged that the future King Charles III sounded "giddily elated" after his ex-wife's death and told Spencer that Diana would be forgotten "soon enough."

The personal and inflammatory nature of the allegations prompted Buckingham Palace-which normally stays quiet when under fire-to put out an opaque statement saying that fraternal grief "can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise."

Meanwhile, Prince Harry, freshly returned to Britain from the U.S. and still estranged from his older brother, Prince William, is weighing options for how best to commemorate the 30th anniversary next summer of their mother's death, a person familiar with the matter said. British media reported he was in talks about making a documentary about her life.

The renewed focus on Diana is a reminder of how the People's Princess remains a potentially kryptonite-like figure for the British monarch. Her treatment during her bitter divorce from Charles and the Windsors' flat-footed response to her death in a Paris car crash have been explored in numerous books, movies and a Netflix television series. For years the episode dented Charles's standing with the British public, which has improved since he became king in 2022.

Spencer-an earl, historian and former NBC journalist-in his book "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" has again swung the spotlight back to that difficult time. Shortly after Diana's death in 1997, Spencer wrote that he spoke by phone to Charles, who he said seemed strangely elated. "Looking back now, I suspect the prince's first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not," Spencer wrote, referring to the now Queen Camilla.

Spencer said that during a separate call he implored Charles not to force William and Harry to walk behind their mother's coffin during a public funeral procession. Charles, he said, reacted angrily. "'Rest assured,' he hissed," Spencer writes. "'We'll forget her soon enough!'" Spencer also claimed that Diana thought that Charles was in love with his valet.

Spencer's motivations for writing the book quickly came under scrutiny, with parts of the British media suggesting Spencer may want to cash in after three divorces. In an interview with the BBC from his family seat at Althorp in central England, he said that both his parents had died in their 60s and that now he was in the autumn of his own life and wanted to set the record straight. "This is my final take on the situation," said Spencer, 62 years old. "I will step off now into the sunset and not be available for comment."

It is no secret that tension existed between Spencer and the monarchy. During a eulogy he delivered in Westminster Abbey after Diana's death, Spencer pledged to his sister that William and Harry's "blood family" would ensure that "their souls are not simply immersed by duty and tradition, but can sing openly as you planned." The remark was taken as a rebuke of the royal family. He ended that speech saying that Diana would "never be extinguished from our minds," a line he now says he included as a retort to Charles's call saying that she would be forgotten. Spencer also said in his book that the royal family's response to Diana's death allowed Harry to subsequently "spin out of control."

Part of the problem for the palace is that Spencer isn't just any old brother-in-law but an aristocrat deeply embedded into the royal fabric. His godmother was Queen Elizabeth II and his brother-in-law was Robert Fellowes, who served as the queen's private secretary in the 1990s. That, in theory, gave him a ringside view into what went on.

"I take what Charles [Spencer] says at face value," says Andrew Morton, who in 1992  wrote a book in secret cooperation with Princess Diana, which threw into the public her failing marriage to the then Prince of Wales.  Morton, however, says Charles was ill-advised to rebut the claims, as it simply further fanned the hype around the memoir.
"He didn't need to tackle this head on," he says, noting that most people will treat the book for what it is: a tribute from a devastated brother to a lost sister.

The accuracy of the book is being questioned. Piers Morgan, a former editor of the Daily Mirror, has called for the first edition of "Swan Song" to be pulped after Spencer wrote that Morgan oversaw the publication of photos of Diana in a leotard at the gym in 1993. Morgan wasn't working at the Mirror or its sister Sunday paper at the time. Given the book included such basic inaccuracies, "how can we believe what he says now about King Charles?" Morgan said. Spencer has issued an apology for the factual error but says he stands by the rest of the book.

Diana's death catapulted her from celebrity divorcee into an almost saintlike figure, whose passing triggered widespread public displays of grief in Britain. It marked the start of a reckoning for the British tabloid media, which was blamed for hounding her after the car in which she was a passenger was chased by paparazzi before crashing. "The massive outpouring around her death has really changed the British psyche, for the better," William said during a magazine interview in 2017.

In the decades since Diana died, the royal family has successfully recast itself in a softer light and as a beacon of patriotic continuity in turbulent times. A poll this summer by YouGov showed that 68% of Britons think that, after nearly four years on the throne, Charles is doing a good job as monarch, his best approval ratings to date.

As the years passed, the frenzy around Diana had mellowed. In 2007, a decade after her death, Harry and William attended a charity rock concert organized in her honor in a packed Wembley Stadium featuring Elton John and Duran Duran. The main members of the royal family were there, with the exception of Camilla, who decided to stay away.

In 2017, it was more low-key, with the brothers creating a memorial garden for her and visiting the gates of Kensington Palace to look at the flowers placed by members of the public. The brothers took part in documentaries describing the events around her death. William said it was the last time he would open up so frankly about what it was like.

By the 25th anniversary of her passing, there was a noticeable royal silence, as Harry had moved to California with his wife Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, and was no longer on speaking terms with William.
Diana's body now rests alone in Spencer's estate at Althorp on an island in the middle of a lake. It is accessible only by rowing boat.
